analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to buy most goods and services from private contractors rather than do the work in-house.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have told every federal agency to obtain its goods and services from private companies, with limited exemptions for work required by law, national security, inherently governmental tasks, or jobs no private company can do. Each year, agencies would have had to submit a schedule for transferring commercial activities to the private sector within five years. The aim, stated in the bill's findings, is to stop "unfair government competition" with private business. In practice, it would have created a large guaranteed market for government contractors and put in-house federal jobs up for transfer.
analysis.who_benefits: Private companies that sell services to the federal government would gain a standing presumption that government work should be theirs, enforced through agency-by-agency transfer schedules. Firms at least 51% owned by an Indian tribe or Native Hawaiian organization would get a specific route to take over converted federal activities. Some taxpayers could benefit if competition genuinely lowers costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each executive, military, and independent agency to obtain all goods and services necessary for or beneficial to its functions from private sources, unless the work is required by law, is inherently governmental, is needed for national defense or homeland security, or has no capable private source [S2] [S3].
Directs each agency to report to Congress a schedule for transferring commercial activities to the private sector to be completed within five years [S3].

Provides that the transfer may happen through divestiture, competitive contracting, conversion to a firm at least 51% owned by an Indian tribe or Native Hawaiian organization, or a public-private competitive sourcing analysis finding private provision is the best value to the taxpayer [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal employees whose work is deemed commercial could have their jobs converted to contractor positions. Taxpayers bear the risk that contracted work, with contractor profit margins and weaker oversight, costs more or is performed worse than in-house work. The bill still requires a best-value analysis before contracting in most cases, but the general rule presumes private provision.

drawbacks.text: The bill's starting presumption is that agencies should buy from private sources and only get out of it by exemption or a best-value finding, which shifts the burden onto keeping work in-house even where in-house performance is cheaper or higher quality [S3].

Contracted work carries contractor profit margins and weaker direct oversight; competitive-sourcing studies under the comparable OMB framework have repeatedly found the promised savings smaller and harder to prove than contractors claim, and critics of outsourcing have warned it hollows out agencies' ability to supervise the contractors themselves.

Agency heads could keep work in-house only by certifying an exemption to Congress under regulations written by the Office of Management and Budget, a process that could be applied loosely in either direction [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's premise that competition saves money is plausible in principle, and it does preserve a best-value analysis before most conversions. But it flips the default: in-house performance becomes something an agency must justify, and every agency must file a five-year transfer schedule. The known problem with large outsourcing mandates is that the cheapest bid often loses money back in oversight, quality problems, and loss of the government's own expertise — a cost that lands on taxpayers and federal workers, while the guaranteed new business lands on contractors. On balance the bill's design serves the contracting industry more than the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no vote was ever taken on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John J. Duncan Jr. introduced the bill on June 3, 2009, with five original cosponsors, all Republicans [S3] [S5].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, which was controlled by Democrats that session, and then on June 26, 2009, to its Subcommittee on Government Management, Organization, and Procurement [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded; the bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In-house federal employees are better off, because the outsourcing mandate never moved and their jobs were not put on a conversion schedule. Contractors did not gain the new standing presumption of private provision. The bill's death is not a public loss, since its main guaranteed beneficiary would have been the contracting industry.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: In-house federal employees kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. John J. Duncan Jr.
for.role: Sponsor, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring agencies to procure goods and services from private sources.

for.name: 9 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining five original cosponsors named in the introduced text.

against.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
against.role: Chair, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never scheduled the bill for consideration; after referral to subcommittee it received no hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: All six original sponsors and all 9 cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic-controlled committee took no action, and no Democrat is recorded in support.

industries.industry: Government contractors and federal services firms
industries.note: The bill makes private provision the default for nearly all federal work and requires each agency to file a five-year schedule for transferring commercial activities out of government employment. Contractors' interest in expanding that channel runs ahead of what a case-by-case best-value analysis would produce.

The bill names firms at least 51% owned by an Indian tribe or Native Hawaiian organization as one of the four approved routes for taking over converted federal activities, giving them a specific path to new contracts.

Work deemed commercial would be put on transfer schedules to private firms, threatening in-house jobs and the agencies' own capacity to supervise contractors. Their interest in keeping work in-house tracks the public interest in accountable, supervised government services.
